newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia markets hit rough, look for anchor.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia markets hit rough, look for anchor.

text.p: Malaysia's financial markets gyrated wildly on Thursday, caught in a continuing battle between speculators and the government.

Stocks plunged to fresh one-and-a-half-year lows, while the ringgit and interbank rates surged, as if on cue from the central bank, which on Wednesday threatened measures, including raising interest rates, to curb speculation in its currency.
The key Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange index slid 2.39 percent to 1,008.52 points, after hitting a low of 1,002.36.
"There has been fierce program selling (of stocks) today," said a senior futures trader at a large local brokerage.

The ringgit ended Thursday at around 2.4900/10 to the dollar after earlier hitting 2.4870/80, its strongest level since May 19. It closed at 2.5033/43 in Kuala Lumpur on Wednesday. "Some big U.S. investment houses were unwinding," said Ishak Ismail, market analyst with research house I.D.E.A. He said the move to 2.4950/dollar triggered heavy stop-loss covering.

Malaysian interbank rates surged across the board, with the benchmark three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR) fixed at 8.38 percent, against 7.92 on Wednesday. The overnight interbank rate surged to 50 percent against 8.0.

Analysts said fear of capital controls helped the ringgit rise, while stock prices fell on across-the-board selling triggered by foreign investors exiting on regional economic fears and better returns elsewhere.
"It is battle, it is not really logical, it is not rational," said Desmond Supple, head of Asian currency research at BZW in Singapore.

"Fundamentally Malaysia compares very favourably with Thailand, but that fact provides little immediate support," he said referring to Thailand recently bowing to market pressure and allowing the baht to float.
"In the current market environment, the onus really is on the authorities to force more clear-headed assessments of risk reward calculations in the ringgit," Supple of BZW said.
But, the analysts said, markets ignored recent supportive comments from Malaysia's leaders.
Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Thursday there was no reason to undermine the ringgit due to the country's stability and its strong economic fundamentals.
The government's Economic Adviser Daim Zainuddin, known widely as an astute stock market investor with a following among retail players, said stock prices were low enough to buy.
"The market is so low it is an opportunity to buy," he told reporters at a fund management conference on Thursday.
Analysts said the Composite Index looked weak technically and may fall further in coming days.

"(A rebound) is less likely to happen soon in Malaysia. It looks to me as though we're going down to about 960," John Schofield, regional technical analyst at Nava SC Securities in Hong Kong, told Reuters Financial Television.
"When there are fears that the central bank will come out to implement capital controls, the market will react negatively," said Kevin Chew, economist at Caspian Securities.
But analysts said the situation did not warrant introduction of capital controls, although some did not totally rule them out.
"Malaysia has done that before and I wouldn't rule it out," said Bernhard Eschweiler, head of economic research (Asia) at J.P. Morgan.

In 1994, faced with a strong flow of hot money into the country, Bank Negara imposed negative interest rates on foreign deposits, banned swaps and stopped foreign investors from buying Malaysian government paper.
On Tuesday, Bank Negara intervened to bolster the ringgit, selling an estimated $1.0 billion.
Ishak of I.D.E.A. said the ringgit was expected to trade to 2.4750 a dollar in the near term.
